Single-stage versus double-stage laryngotracheal reconstruction for grade III subglottic stenosis in children: a multicenter cohort

Ana Silva, Bruno Souza, Carla Costa, Pediatric Airway Group

Abstract

Background

The best strategy for grade III subglottic stenosis is debated.

Methods

Retrospective cohort of 84 children (2015-2024) across 3 centers.

Results

Decannulation was achieved in 88% after single-stage and 91% after double-stage reconstruction (p=0.62).

Conclusions

Single-stage reconstruction had similar decannulation with shorter stay.

Introduction

Grade III subglottic stenosis in children is most often acquired after prolonged intubation in the neonatal unit, and its repair remains one of the more demanding operations in paediatric airway surgery. Laryngotracheal reconstruction with costal cartilage grafts can be done in a single stage, with a period of intubation as the stent, or in two stages, with the tracheostomy kept until the graft has healed.

Both strategies are in use, and the choice between them still depends more on the habits of each centre than on comparative data. Earlier series were small, came from single centres and reported decannulation with different definitions, which makes them hard to compare.

Methods

We reviewed every child who underwent laryngotracheal reconstruction for grade III stenosis on the Myer-Cotton scale in three tertiary centres between January 2015 and December 2024. Children with glottic involvement, complete tracheal rings or a previous open procedure were excluded, and the remaining 84 formed the cohort.

The primary outcome was decannulation within 12 months, defined as the tracheostomy removed and not replaced for 30 days. Secondary outcomes were the length of hospital stay, the number of endoscopic procedures after the operation and the need for revision surgery. Groups were compared with Fisher's exact test and the Mann-Whitney test, and a logistic model adjusted for age, weight and comorbidity.

Results

Forty-one children had single-stage and 43 had double-stage reconstruction. Median age was 3.1 years in the single-stage group and 2.7 years in the double-stage group, and comorbidity was similar between the groups.

Decannulation within 12 months was achieved in 36 of 41 children after single-stage reconstruction and in 39 of 43 after double-stage reconstruction. Single-stage patients left hospital a median of four days earlier, and needed fewer endoscopies in the first year. Revision surgery was required in five children in each group.

Discussion

In this multicentre cohort, single-stage reconstruction reached a decannulation rate similar to the staged approach while shortening the stay in hospital. The difference in stay reflects the time in intensive care after extubation more than the operation itself, and it should be weighed against the risks of sedation in a small airway.

The retrospective design means that the choice of strategy was not random: surgeons tended to stage the reconstruction in children with more comorbidity, which the adjusted model only partly corrects. A prospective comparison with a common definition of success would settle the question.
